transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Ever since my husband’s diagnosis, I feel like I’m reacting to everything in a way I can’t manage, and it’s starting to interfere with how I function at work and at home. It just feels like too much for me to handle on my own right now.
Since your husband’s diagnosis, have you had unwanted memories, nightmares, or felt like you were reliving the moment you found out? Do you also find yourself avoiding reminders of it?

No, I haven't experienced any nightmares, flashbacks, or feelings of reliving that moment, nor am I avoiding reminders of it. In fact, I've been highly focused on managing his care and coordinating all of his appointments. It is more that I'm feeling completely overwhelmed by the daily reality of handling everything.

Over the past 2 weeks, have you been feeling down or losing interest in things most of the day nearly every day, or is it mainly constant uncontrollable worry about your husband and everything you need to manage?

It is definitely more of a constant worry and feeling completely wound up about managing everything. While I’ve stopped doing my hiking and yoga, it’s not because I’ve lost interest, but because I feel too anxious and guilty to enjoy them while my mind is constantly running through worst-case scenarios.
Before your husband’s diagnosis, were you already someone who worried excessively about many different parts of life for at least 6 months, or did this anxiety begin mainly after his diagnosis?

No, this intense anxiety and worry started specifically after my husband's diagnosis about three months ago. Before that, I wasn't an excessive worrier at all; I was generally very organized and managed my stress well through my hobbies like hiking, yoga, and knitting. This level of overwhelm is completely new to me.
How soon after your husband’s diagnosis did these symptoms start, and have they been causing clear problems in your work, relationships, or daily responsibilities?

The symptoms started within just a few weeks of his diagnosis and have been building over the last two months. They've caused real problems at work, where my concentration has slipped so much that my supervisor called me in over inspection errors and gave me a tense performance review. I’ve also completely withdrawn from my hiking group and yoga classes, which used to be my main sources of support and stress relief.

Has your reaction felt much stronger than what you or others would expect for your husband’s diagnosis, or does it feel like a proportionate response that has just become hard to manage? Also, have there been any other major stressors around the same time that might be contributing?

Yes, it definitely feels like a switch flipped and I'm overreacting in ways I wouldn't expect, like snapping at my coworkers over tiny mistakes and crying in my car after his appointments. On top of his diagnosis, we are currently going through a major quality audit at my manufacturing plant, and I've been working extra hours to make up for missed time, which has added a massive amount of pressure.

What was your husband diagnosed with, and would most people in your situation see it as a life-threatening or catastrophic event? Also, since this started, have you had panic attacks or thoughts that life is not worth living?

My husband was diagnosed with early-stage Parkinson’s disease; it is a serious, progressive condition that has turned our lives upside down, but it isn't an immediate, life-threatening emergency. I haven't experienced any panic attacks or thoughts of ending my life, but I am just extremely overwhelmed, irritable, and unable to sleep or relax.

final_diagnosis.reason: Symptoms began within weeks of an identifiable psychosocial stressor (husband’s Parkinson’s diagnosis, compounded by work audit), are characterized mainly by anxiety, overwhelm, irritability, insomnia, and impaired concentration, and have caused clear occupational and social impairment. PTSD is not supported because there are no re-experiencing or avoidance symptoms and the stressor is not described as catastrophic/life-threatening in the required sense. GAD is less likely because the excessive worry was not longstanding and started specifically after the stressor.
